strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: identifies genuine limitation of AE pretraining creating task-mismatch between reconstruction and downstream objectives
Simple and interpretable approach using semantically-grounded anchor tokens from context, avoiding learning compression tokens from scratch
Comprehensive evaluation: consistent improvements across multiple compression ratios (5x, 15x, 51x), in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA datasets, demonstrating strong generalization
Thorough ablation studies validating necessity of each component (bidirectional attention, anchor embeddings) and robustness to token selection strategies
Practical efficiency gains: 31% faster training than ICAE, 26% faster than baselines, with best perplexity (10.79)
Good analysis with attention visualizations showing interpretable differences in learned patterns and representation space analysis demonstrating semantic proximity maintenance
High reproducibility: code promised, detailed hyperparameters and clear implementation details provided
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (token selection from existing literature, standard bidirectional attention from BERT/recent work, simple additive anchor embeddings) without strong innovation
Narrow evaluation scope: only Llama-3.2-1B model tested (unclear scalability to 7B+) and only QA tasks evaluated (no summarization, classification, or other applications)

Bidirectional-causal attention mismatch under-discussed: encoder uses bidirectional attention during compression but target LLM uses causal attention during inference; no ablation or deep analysis of this train-test discrepancy
Missing inference cost analysis: only training time compared; computational overhead of bidirectional attention during compression and end-to-end latency not characterized

Token selection analysis incomplete: simple uniform strategy used without establishing optimality; similar performance of Lingua-2 selection (Table 4) somewhat undermines claim that anchor tokens inherently contain sufficient information
Incomplete mechanistic understanding: no analysis of which tokens are selected, their semantic properties, or why anchor tokens maintain representation proximity to context tokens
Representation similarity argument under-validated: Figure 5 shows proximity in KV space, but correlation between this and downstream performance is not rigorously established
AE effect analysis complications: Table 5 shows inconsistency with original ICAE findings; raises questions about whether criticisms are universal or method-specific
No statistical significance testing: no error bars or confidence intervals reported; unclear if improvements are statistically significant across runs

Comparison fairness concerns: fundamentally different architecture (select from context vs. create new tokens) may not be entirely comparable; unclear whether improvements come from anchor selection or other design choices

strengths: Clear problem motivation identifying AE task misalignment with downstream objectives
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple compression ratios and datasets with proper in-domain/OOD splits
Thorough ablation studies examining component contributions and design choices
Consistent empirical improvements across all tested conditions
Helpful visualization analysis including attention maps and representation analysis
Code and hyperparameters promised for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is combining existing techniques (original tokens + bidirectional attention + anchor embeddings); individual components are not novel
Unfair architectural comparison: SAC inherently has advantage by using semantically pre-aligned original context tokens vs. random special tokens; this fundamental difference is underemphasized
Narrow experimental scope: tested only on 1B model, single task domain (QA only), single LLM family; generalization to larger models and other tasks unknown
Modest and potentially insignificant improvements: 1-3 EM point gains without statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple runs
Oversimplified claims about autoencoding: Table 5 shows mixed results; paper doesn't clearly distinguish whether benefits come from architectural design or pre-semantic-alignment of original tokens
Confusion between token selection and compression: no clear analysis of information loss, comparison to pure selection methods, or what is actually being compressed
Token selection strategy underexplored: uniform selection borrowed from EPL; Table 4 shows Lingua-2 performs nearly identically, suggesting strategy selection matters less than claimed
Representation analysis limitations: t-SNE visualizations misleading about quality; 'closer to original' doesn't prove 'better for downstream' and could indicate less compression
Missing statistical rigor: no significance testing, no multiple runs, no error analysis despite modest improvement margins
Limited scope of related work: insufficient comparison to token pruning literature, other efficient inference methods, and pure token selection approaches

strengths: Clear problem motivation: Identifies genuine mismatch between AE-based optimization and downstream task requirements
Elegant solution: Using original context tokens as anchors is simple, intuitive, and naturally provides semantic grounding without training from scratch
Comprehensive evaluation: 13 QA datasets across 3 compression ratios with consistent improvements, especially strong gains at higher ratios (36.2% EM improvement on OOD at 5x)
Thorough ablation studies: Systematically validates each component (bidirectional attention, anchor embeddings, token selection, AE effects) with substantial performance impacts

Insightful analysis: Attention visualization, t-SNE representation analysis, and training curves provide understanding of why SAC works; representations naturally cluster close to original context tokens
Practical efficiency: ~31% faster training than ICAE, lower perplexity, avoids LLM finetuning requirement
Well-executed presentation: Clear writing, good figures, comprehensive tables, and proper experimental documentation
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Combines existing components (anchor embeddings, bidirectional attention from NV-Embed/LLM2Vec, token selection from EPL); primary contribution is the combination, which is incremental for top-tier venues

Narrow experimental scope: Single downstream task (QA only—no summarization, generation, dialogue), single model scale (1B only—not tested on 7B, 13B+), limited compression setting (510-token chunks, not truly long contexts)

No large-scale validation: Context compression primarily addresses long-context LLMs, but evaluation lacks realistic long-context scenarios (10k+ tokens) and larger models where compression value is greatest
Train-test attention mismatch: Bidirectional attention used during training/encoding but causal attention during inference; this distribution shift is noted but not thoroughly analyzed or ablated

Overstated conclusions about autoencoding: Claims AE is 'not entirely essential' based on Table 5, but SAC(w/AE+LM) only slightly underperforms SAC (62.04 vs 63.63 F1); argument primarily shows AE unnecessary for SAC architecture rather than harmful to compression generally
Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; some improvements modest (e.g., 51x OOD: 32.24 vs 30.22 for EPL)
Missing inference analysis: No inference latency or memory measurements despite efficiency being key motivation; computational overhead of using multi-layer KV pairs not discussed
Token selection underexplored: Uniform middle-token strategy seems potentially suboptimal compared to importance-weighted selection; limited exploration of why this works or how it generalizes
Incomplete error analysis: No discussion of failure modes, types of contexts where SAC excels/fails, or examples demonstrating method effectiveness
Implementation details unclear: Exact bidirectional attention modification not fully specified; sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., anchor embedding dimensions) not explored

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 12 QA datasets, 3 compression ratios, and multiple model sizes with consistent improvements (6-7% F1 at 15× compression)
Thorough ablations and analysis including component ablations, AE effect studies, attention visualization, representation analysis, and gradient orthogonality investigation
Practical advantages: 26-31% faster training than baselines, comparable or better inference efficiency, and released code/data for reproducibility
Clear motivation identifying AE-LM gradient orthogonality as a problem, with empirical evidence in Figure 9 providing actionable insights
Simple and generalizable method that works with different token selection strategies and scales well to larger models (1B to 8B)
Strong baselines and fair comparisons with ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL, and other recent compression methods
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combines existing ideas (token selection + bidirectional attention) without fundamental innovation; the paper itself acknowledges combining prior methods
Unaddressed train-test mismatch: anchor tokens trained with bidirectional attention but deployed with causal attention during inference; no analysis of this architectural inconsistency or its effects

Unfair baseline comparison with EPL: SAC builds on EPL's position layout (acknowledged in footnote) but lacks ablations isolating which improvements come from real tokens vs. embeddings vs. bidirectional attention

Incomplete AE analysis: gradient orthogonality signal has high variance (Figure 9), and results show SAC(ae+lm) outperforms SAC on small datasets (Table 20-QMSum), contradicting the universal AE removal narrative

Moderate empirical improvements: 6-7% F1 at 15× compression and 2.5% out-of-domain are solid but not dramatic; at higher compression ratios (51×) improvements shrink to 2%, suggesting limited gains in extreme scenarios

Weak theoretical justification: intuitive explanations provided (natural semantic priors) but no principled reasoning for why real tokens + embeddings + bidirectional attention should be fundamentally superior to learned compression tokens
Missing critical ablation: no isolated comparison of 'EPL + bidirectional attention' to fairly decompose the contribution of each component
Long-context results underwhelm: Tables 20-21 show marginal improvements on 32K/24K tasks, with SAC(ae+lm) sometimes better, undermining the core narrative

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation with consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks (MRQA in-domain/OOD, different compression ratios, model scales 1B-8B)
Solid experimental design with thorough ablation studies, representation analysis, and attention visualization providing good post-hoc insights
Practical efficiency gains (26-31% faster training, lower FLOPs) despite bidirectional attention, showing good engineering
Clear problem motivation: autoencoding objectives may conflict with downstream tasks (supported by gradient orthogonality analysis)
Reproducible work with released code, models, and detailed hyperparameters
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: anchor embeddings are trivial (learnable vector addition), bidirectional attention is from prior work (NV-Embed, LLM2Vec), and token selection strategy directly follows EPL

Weak theoretical justification: gradient orthogonality in Figure 9 doesn't prove AE is harmful; Table 5 shows inconsistent evidence (AE+LM sometimes outperforms LM-only at 5× compression), contradicting the core narrative
Modest improvements over strongest baseline EPL: ~3.3% F1 in-domain and ~2.5% F1 out-of-domain at 15× compression—insufficient margins for top-tier venue

Unclear architectural decisions: bidirectional attention only during encoding (not decoding) raises questions about how encoder benefits propagate to decoder; anchor embeddings' necessity unexplained; no justification for using original tokens over learned anchors

Token selection analysis undermines core claims: Table 4 shows informed selection (Lingua-2) performs nearly identically to uniform selection, suggesting token selection isn't the bottleneck and 'semantic anchors' may be a misnomer
Incomplete ablations: no isolation of contribution from removing AE vs. architectural changes; unclear which components drive improvements; interaction effects not studied
Limited evaluation scope: only QA and summarization tasks; only Llama models tested; modest model sizes (1B-8B); missing comparisons with recent methods and learned selection approaches
Inconsistent evidence on AE harm: method not consistently better without AE; why AE helps at 5× but hurts at 15× is unexplained; contradicts the primary motivation

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: articulates genuine limitation of AE-based compression objectives conflicting with downstream tasks, supported by empirical analysis

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple datasets (MRQA 6 tasks in-domain and out-of-domain, summarization), compression ratios (5x, 15x, 51x), and model scales (1B, 3B, 8B) demonstrate consistent improvements of 6.7-23.5% F1 over EPL
Practical efficiency advantages: 31% faster training than ICAE, lower inference latency despite bidirectional attention, and better pretraining perplexity (10.79 vs 10.88)

Thorough analysis and ablation studies: Component ablations show necessity of both anchor embeddings and bidirectional attention; attention visualizations reveal focused token patterns; representation analysis (Figure 4) demonstrates alignment with original context space
Simple and elegant architecture: Method avoids redundant special tokens and complex pretraining, using straightforward modifications to standard LLM inference
Strong cross-domain generalization: Consistent performance gains on both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations across multiple datasets
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Anchor token selection resembles existing methods (SelectiveContext, LLMLingua), bidirectional attention is well-established, and anchor embeddings are straightforward. Contribution is primarily architectural combination rather than novel components

Shallow analysis of why AE is problematic: Gradient orthogonality (Figure 9) shown only for SAC, not baselines. Intuitive explanation about limited capacity is somewhat hand-wavy. Table 5 shows mixed results across architectures, undermining claim that AE is universally suboptimal

Token selection strategy under-explored: Default uniform selection borrowed from EPL; Table 4 shows minimal differences between random, Lingua-2, and uniform strategies; limited evidence supporting claim that SAC effectively leverages any token selection strategy

Narrow evaluation scope: Experiments limited to QA and summarization tasks; no evaluation on retrieval, reasoning, or other long-context applications. All experiments use Llama+LoRA; generalization to other architectures unclear. Long-context improvements modest (14.95 vs 14.82 on QMSum)

Experimental confounds: Training on 510-token contexts but testing on 32K tokens creates distribution shift. Table 21 shows SAC(ae+lm) sometimes outperforms SAC, suggesting AE's role is task/context-dependent rather than universally harmful

Incomplete architectural ablations: SAC vs EPL comparison conflates anchor embeddings and bidirectional attention. Would benefit from incremental addition studies rather than component removal ablations

Limited depth of mechanistic understanding: Why do anchor embeddings help semantically rich tokens? Attention patterns are visualized but not deeply analyzed. Representation alignment is shown but causal mechanism unexplained

Overstated claims: 'Autoencoding-free' is highlighted but method architecturally similar to prior work with primarily different training objective. 'Inherently understands context' overstates contribution relative to language modeling pretraining requirement
